edits.find:
Three bedside facts close this before any lesion is considered. He is working to breathe — grunting, flaring, retracting — and cyanotic heart disease produces comfortable tachypnea, not distress. His saturation rises from 65% to 92% on oxygen, which cannot happen in d-transposition, where systemic flow bypasses the lungs entirely. And the two limbs read the same, so nothing is shunting right-to-left across the duct. That leaves parenchymal disease, and a 32-week infant with ground-glass opacification and air bronchograms has surfactant deficiency: respiratory distress syndrome.

When the examination is instead a list of normals — no murmur, symmetric pulses, equal four-extremity pressures, clear lungs, no retractions, no stridor — the sort has already excluded lung and heart, and the remaining finding is temporal. What brings the cyanosis on, and what relieves it, is then the whole question: cyanosis on latching that clears with crying is nasal obstruction, because neonates are obligate nasal breathers and crying opens the oral airway. The inverse pattern — cyanosis worsened by crying — is a tet spell.

edits.find: Every respiratory finding here is real and every one of them is downstream. The deciding findings are cardiac and there are three: a gallop, a new holosystolic murmur at the apex, and 1+ pulses with a blood pressure of 60/40. A gallop is an S3, a ventricle taking volume it cannot handle. An apical holosystolic murmur in this setting is mitral regurgitation from ventricular dilation, not a primary valve lesion. The viral prodrome is the cause, not a coincidence: coxsackievirus B and adenovirus are the usual agents, and myocyte injury is part direct and part immune-mediated.
